confirmed.title: NOT_SENT / DEFINITIVE_REJECT_ZERO_FILL releases a leg whose CID already possibly or provably reached the venue
confirmed.requirement: NG-DB-005, NG-HIST-004, AC-56 (also AC-16/AC-17: UNKNOWN keeps reservation, no new CID)
confirmed.failure_scenario: (a) First submit returns UNKNOWN (timeout), so the order may be resting on the venue. The engine re-dispatches the same CID with mark_dispatching(resend_same_cid=True), and the second call hits connector pre-send validation (NOT_SENT) or a venue 'duplicate client id' reject (DEFINITIVE_REJECT_ZERO_FILL). record_transport_result moves the leg to REJECTED_UNSENT/REJECTED_ZERO_FILL, releases the reservation, cycle_release_blockers returns [], and _check_single_physical_entry accepts a new ENTRY revision with a new CID. Result: a possibly live first order is no longer tracked or reserved, and duplicate exposure follows. (b) An active-orders poll records the order (record_order_evidence, then set_leg_state LIVE) before the transport result is written. A later NOT_SENT still makes the leg REJECTED_UNSENT and releases its reservation.
confirmed.evidence: The only guard is `if entry.status == "PENDING" and outcome != NOT_SENT` (line 2747). Any DISPATCHED row accepts NOT_SENT/DEFINITIVE_REJECT, whatever `attempts` says, an earlier UNKNOWN outcome, or order.last_evidence_ms / LIVE state. Only fills are checked (line 2758). Probe output: after UNKNOWN, resend, NOT_SENT: `OrderState.REJECTED_UNSENT reservations: [] release blockers: []`, and a new entry revision got cid 1099511627778. The same happens with DEFINITIVE_REJECT_ZERO_FILL ('duplicate client order id'): `REJECTED_ZERO_FILL []`. For a LIVE leg with a recorded active venue row, NOT_SENT gives `REJECTED_UNSENT reservations: [] blockers: []`.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Accept NOT_SENT/DEFINITIVE_REJECT only for a row's first dispatch (attempts == 1, with no earlier UNKNOWN outcome). Refuse them, or record a durable conflict, when the leg is past SUBMIT_UNKNOWN or has venue evidence (last_evidence_ms, exchange_order_id, ACCEPTED). In every other case keep SUBMIT_UNKNOWN and the reservation.

verdict.reasoning:
I confirmed the claim in the code and with a probe.

**The code path** (store.py):
1. `mark_dispatching(..., resend_same_cid=True)` (lines 2656-2690) accepts a DONE/UNKNOWN row. It sets `status='DISPATCHED'`, increments `attempts`, and overwrites the earlier `outcome` with NULL (line 2675). After that, the row no longer records that the first send timed out; only `attempts` shows it.
2. `record_transport_result` (lines 2723-2798) guards only against a non-NOT_SENT result on a PENDING row (line 2747) and against fills (lines 2758-2760). A DISPATCHED row accepts NOT_SENT or DEFINITIVE_REJECT_ZERO_FILL whatever `attempts` says, and whatever venue evidence the order already has.
3. The leg then moves to REJECTED_UNSENT or REJECTED_ZERO_FILL. `_set_leg_state_raw` (lines 2362-2368) releases the reservation for any final state.

**Probe.** I used the branch's own test support (`Env`, `FakeTransport`, `record_entry_intent`, `submit_via_protocol`). Steps: first submit returns UNKNOWN("timeout"), then `mark_dispatching(resend_same_cid=True)`, then NOT_SENT. Result: `OrderState.REJECTED_UNSENT`, reservations `[]`, `cycle_release_blockers` `[]`. `prepare_submit` for ENTRY revision=1 then got a new CID, 1099511627778 (the old one was ...777). DEFINITIVE_REJECT_ZERO_FILL gave the same result: `REJECTED_ZERO_FILL`, `[]`, `[]`, and a new CID.

**Spec conflict.**
- NG-DB-005: only a pre-send rejection proving transport was never called releases an "unsent intent". Timeout keeps UNKNOWN and the reservation.
- AC-56: timeout stays UNKNOWN and creates no new CID or revision.
- NG-HIST-004: no new ID after a timeout.

A NOT_SENT on the second attempt proves only that the second call never happened. It says nothing about the first, timed-out call, which may be resting on the venue. The store's own docstring presents NOT_SENT as "proven no transport call". The store is the only component that holds the attempt history, and it erases the UNKNOWN outcome, so it is the right place for this guard. The engine is not.

**Scope.** This is persistence-layer enforcement of NG-DB-005 and AC-56 inside store.py, so it is in scope. It is not handled elsewhere: no test covers resend followed by NOT_SENT or reject.

**Why severity is reduced.** The main scenario, (a), needs the engine to use `resend_same_cid`. The contract gates that on documented venue idempotence of the CID. Lighter may not document it, which would make the path rare in this deployment. Under genuine idempotence, a definitive reject on the resend arguably does refer to the CID; a NOT_SENT does not. Scenario (b) needs contradictory inputs: active venue evidence for the order and a NOT_SENT for the same dispatch. That is a defensive gap, not a normal flow.

The consequence is serious: a possibly live order stops being tracked or reserved, and a new ENTRY revision gets a new CID, which means duplicate exposure. But the reachability preconditions narrow it, so I rate it medium rather than high.

confirmed.title: mark_dispatching silently re-authorises transport for an already DISPATCHED (unknown-outcome) row without resend_same_cid, even when degraded
confirmed.requirement: NG-HIST-004 (same-ID repeat only with documented venue idempotence, otherwise UNKNOWN), NG-DB-002 (Unknown does not lead to blind retry), AC-16, AC-55
confirmed.failure_scenario: The process dies after transport was called but before the result committed, leaving the outbox row DISPATCHED. On restart the engine walks unresolved_outbox() and calls mark_dispatching(tx, id) the same way it does for PENDING rows. For the DISPATCHED row the call succeeds, returns status DISPATCHED and leaves attempts at 1, so under the protocol the engine is cleared to call transport and sends the same CID again without the explicit resend flag. The durable attempts counter under-counts the real sends. The early return also comes before the degraded check, so a degraded store still authorises this SUBMIT.
confirmed.evidence: `if entry.status == "DISPATCHED": return entry` (lines 2667-2668) runs before the `resend_same_cid` requirement (2669-2671) and before the degraded guard (2675-2676). Probe: crash armed at 'after_transport' (1 submit sent), then reopen and `mark_dispatching(tx, ob.id)` with no flag returned `DISPATCHED attempts 1`. By contrast, test_unknown_submit_keeps_reservation_and_same_cid_resend_only_explicit shows that the DONE/UNKNOWN row is refused without the flag.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Treat a DISPATCHED row like DONE/UNKNOWN: refuse re-dispatch unless resend_same_cid=True, increment attempts, and apply the degraded check first. If in-process idempotence is needed, key it on a per-process dispatch token rather than on status alone.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute the store behaviour. At 39022a497 the code is unchanged in the worktree HEAD. In store.py, mark_dispatching has `if entry.status == "DISPATCHED": return entry` at lines 2667-2668. That return comes before the resend_same_cid check for DONE rows (2669-2671) and before the degraded-SUBMIT guard (2675-2676).

I reproduced it with a scratch pytest. I armed a crash at after_transport, reopened the store, and got one unresolved row that is DISPATCHED with attempts=1 and transport_possibly_invoked=True. Calling mark_dispatching(tx, id) with no flag returned DISPATCHED with attempts=1. Calling it again with resend_same_cid=True also returned attempts=1, and the dispatch time was not refreshed.

The store treats this call as the gate for sending the same CID again. Its docstring says transport may only be called after mark_dispatching commits, and resend_same_cid is "only allowed when the engine relies on documented venue idempotence". test_unknown_submit_keeps_reservation_and_same_cid_resend_only_explicit enforces this for DONE/UNKNOWN rows, with the comment "no blind retry". A DISPATCHED row after a restart is the same maybe-sent state, as the unresolved_outbox docstring and transport_possibly_invoked=True both say. Yet the gate lets it through without the flag. This is the store side of NG-HIST-004 ("the same ID may be repeated only with documented venue idempotence").

Transactions stay open while the store is degraded. So a row left DISPATCHED after a record_transport_result commit fails gets success from mark_dispatching instead of the PersistenceError that PENDING and DONE/UNKNOWN rows get. Even the documented flagged resend path is affected: it skips the degraded guard and does not record the extra send in attempts.

I lowered the severity from high to medium for three reasons:
- No engine code exists in this workstream.
- The actual double send needs an engine that treats a successful return as permission for a DISPATCHED row. The WS-B handoff (trace/ws-b-store.md, lines 91-93) tells the engine that DISPATCHED rows stay SUBMIT_UNKNOWN and are re-sent only with resend_same_cid=True.
- The claim's reference to NG-DB-002 does not fit this case. That clause forbids blind retry with a new ID, not the same one.

Still, the store-level inconsistency is concretely reachable, including through the legitimate flagged path.

confirmed.title: Default paths put both prior-run markers inside the same data directory as the DB, so wiping it yields a fresh bootstrap, reused CIDs and a newly adopted baseline
confirmed.requirement: AC-54, NG-DB-004 (missing DB with prior-run evidence is not created clean and does not take the current position as B), NG-HIST-004/AC-43 (unique CID)
confirmed.failure_scenario: Deployment with the documented defaults (path None, lock_dir None) and no prior_run_markers callback, which is optional and defaults to None. The operator loses or deletes <data>/neutral_grid, which holds the DB, <db>.marker.json and locks/<key>.marker.json. NeutralGridStore.open(..., create_if_missing=True) finds no evidence and creates a fresh DB with cid_epoch 1. bootstrap() accepts a new B as a first bootstrap, and the first allocated CID equals the lost DB's first CID.
confirmed.evidence: default_lock_dir -> `base/"neutral_grid"/"locks"` (line 451); default_db_path -> `base/"neutral_grid"/...sqlite3` (line 459). Probe with these defaults under a scratch base: after `rmtree(base/'neutral_grid')` the reopen reported `bootstrapped False recovered_from_loss False epoch 1`, then `old cid 1099511627777 new cid 1099511627777 reused: True baseline now 0`. test_wiped_data_directory_still_blocked_by_host_marker passes only because Env puts locks at tmp/locks, outside tmp/data.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Put the host marker in a location independent of the DB data directory by default, or make a venue-evidence prior_run_markers callback mandatory whenever create_if_missing=True. Also consider deriving the fresh-DB epoch from venue-observed CIDs.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this claim. The code does what the claim says, and I reproduced it.

**What the code does**
- `default_lock_dir()` (store.py:447-451) returns `data_path()/neutral_grid/locks`.
- `default_db_path()` (store.py:454-459) returns `data_path()/neutral_grid/<key>.sqlite3`.
- `open()` falls back to these defaults at lines 1217 and 1219.
- `_marker_paths` (line 1335-1336) puts one marker next to the DB and one in the lock dir. With the defaults, both markers sit under the same `<data>/neutral_grid` tree.
- `_prior_run_evidence` (line 1339-1356) only looks at those markers, leftover `-wal`/`-shm`/`-journal` files and the optional callback. `prior_run_markers` defaults to `None`, even though CONTRACTS.md lists `prior_run_markers: callable` as a parameter with no default.
- With no evidence, `_initialise` (line 1404) sets `cid_epoch = 1` and `recovered_from_loss = 0`.

**Reproduction**
I used a scratch base with `default_db_path(IDENTITY, base)` and `default_lock_dir(base)`, then:
1. `open(create_if_missing=True)` gave epoch 1.
2. `rmtree(base/'neutral_grid')`.
3. `open(create_if_missing=True)` succeeded with "after wipe epoch 1 recovered False".

The new DB therefore restarts the old CID sequence, and `bootstrap()` would accept a new baseline B as if this were the first run.

**Why the test does not cover it**
`test_wiped_data_directory_still_blocked_by_host_marker` passes only because `Env` puts the locks at `tmp/locks`, outside `tmp/data/neutral_grid`. The trace doc cites this test for AC-54, but the protection it tests does not exist with the default paths. The "host" marker is not independent of the DB directory there. This contradicts the module docstring ("a database recreated after loss gets a new epoch so CIDs of the lost database are never reused") and weakens the NG-DB-004 / AC-54 gate.

**Why severity drops to low**
- The venue-evidence callback exists. The WS-D handoff (trace ws-b-store.md, around line 80) tells the engine to pass one ("venue has orders/trades with our CID epoch"). If WS-D does, venue evidence blocks the fresh DB.
- For CID reuse, `allocate_cid` fails closed with `CidCollisionError` on a CID the engine has recorded via `note_foreign_cids` or flags via `is_foreign_cid`.
- The new B still needs an explicit operator confirmation in `bootstrap()`.

So the failure needs the whole default `neutral_grid` directory wiped (operator reset or lost data volume) and an integration that leaves out the optional callback. That can happen with the store's own defaults, but it is not the only safeguard.

confirmed.title: Late fill after cycle release creates an obligation that can never be covered by a TP and disappears from the restart view
confirmed.requirement: NG-HIST-002 (late evidence after reuse belongs to the old cycle), NG-CELL-003 (late fill creates a TP obligation of the old cycle), NG-DB-003 step 6 (restart restores TP obligations), AC-42/AC-52
confirmed.failure_scenario: Entry of 10 fills 6, is canceled and proven TERMINAL; TP 6 fills and the cycle is closed COMPLETE. A late 2-LIT trade on the old entry is then applied to the COMPLETE cycle (E=8, X=6) with LATE_FILL and CUMULATIVE conflicts. After the operator audit, allocate_cid and record_intent both refuse a TP for the closed cycle ('cycle ... is not open'). load_state().open_cycles omits it, so a restarted engine never sees the obligation. grid_mutation_blockers() returns [] even while the LATE_FILL conflict is unresolved, so migrate_grid proceeds despite its docstring. The 2-LIT obligation is orphaned.
confirmed.evidence: load_state uses open_cycles() (state='OPEN') at line 3700. allocate_cid raises for non-OPEN cycles (2262-2263); record_intent raises 'intent for a closed cycle' (2512-2513). grid_mutation_blockers only scans `state = 'OPEN'` cycles (1951). Probe: `old cycle COMPLETE E 8 X 6 conflicts ['LATE_FILL', 'CUMULATIVE_EXCEEDS_ORDER']`, `open cycles in load_state: []`, `grid mutation blockers: []`, `TP for late obligation refused: InvalidTransitionError cycle grid-a/3/1 is not open`.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Let a late fill on a COMPLETE cycle reopen it or mark it as having an outstanding obligation that allows TP allocation after audit. Include cycles with entry_filled != exit_filled or late_evidence != 0 in load_state, and include them plus unresolved conflicts in grid_mutation_blockers.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute the claim. The code at 39022a497 behaves as described, and I reproduced the scenario. The worktree HEAD is 41d347fd6, but its store.py diff from 39022a497 only touches the `dedupe_keys` and `write_snapshot` paths, so the result applies to the reviewed commit.

What the code does:
- **Late fill is recorded:** `_apply_trade` (store_39022 ~3061-3088) sets `late = leg.final or cycle.state == "COMPLETE"`. It credits `entry_filled` on the old cycle through `_credit_cycle`, sets `late_evidence=1` and raises a `LATE_FILL` conflict. So the store expects late fills on released cycles.
- **No TP path afterwards:** every route to a TP for that quantity is closed.
  - `allocate_cid` (2262-2263) raises "cycle ... is not open".
  - `record_intent` (2512-2513) raises "intent for a closed cycle".
  - `_insert_allocations` raises "allocation to a closed cycle", so a TP of the next generation cannot carry an allocation to the old cycle either.
  - The only cycle transition is OPEN->COMPLETE; nothing reopens a cycle.
  - `record_manual_reconciliation` only sets `late_evidence=2` and resolves conflicts. `record_baseline_audit` explicitly leaves cell obligations untouched.
- **Obligation is invisible:** `load_state` builds its view from `open_cycles()` (state='OPEN'). `grid_mutation_blockers` scans only OPEN cycles and does not look at unresolved conflicts, so `migrate_grid` is not blocked.

Probe run (read-only, temp DB in the scratchpad), same flow as the claim: entry 10 fills 6, canceled and proven TERMINAL; TP 6 filled and TERMINAL; `close_cycle` gives COMPLETE; then a late trade of 2 on the old entry.
- Output: `old cycle COMPLETE E 8 X 6 late 1 conflicts ['LATE_FILL','CUMULATIVE_EXCEEDS_ORDER']`.
- After `record_manual_reconciliation` resolves those conflicts, `entry_blockers` is `[]`.
- `load_state` open cycles: `[]`. `grid_mutation_blockers`: `[]`.
- A TP revision 1 for gen 1 is refused with "cycle grid-a/3/1 is not open".
- `open_cycle` gen 2 succeeds, and a gen-2 TP allocated to gen 1 is refused with "allocation to a closed cycle".
- The position ledger shows buys 8 / sells 6. So 2 LIT of exposure has no TP path and does not appear in the restart view.

Why this breaks the spec:
- NG-CELL-003: a late fill after cancel "creates a new TP obligation of the old cycle".
- AC-08: the late history fill increases the obligation "and is covered by TP".
- NG-HIST-002 explicitly expects late evidence after reuse to belong to the old cycle, with a freeze only until audit.
- NG-DB-003 step 6: restart must restore TP obligations.

The store records the obligation but offers no way to cover or restore it, even after the audit. The trace row for AC-42 claims "late fill after terminal/release goes to the old cycle", but its tests only cover a cycle that is terminal and still OPEN, not a released one.

Why medium and not higher: the case is rare (the fill has to arrive after the settlement delay and repeat scan), and the market does freeze until the operator audits it. But after the audit the exposure has no TP and a restarted engine does not see it.

confirmed.title: The same-host single-writer lock sits under the per-checkout data_path, so two checkouts can run two engines on one account and market
confirmed.failure_scenario: default_lock_dir() is <data_path()>/neutral_grid/locks, and hummingbot.data_path() is <checkout root>/data. The same host has two checkouts or worktrees, or two containers with their own data volumes. Each launches the engine for the same account and market. Each takes its own flock on a different lock file and opens its own DB, so both engines trade the same account. Both DBs start at cid_epoch 1, so their CIDs also collide.
confirmed.evidence: store.py:447-451 builds the lock dir from data_path(). hummingbot/__init__.py:52-56 sets data_path = realpath(prefix_path()/data), and prefix_path is the repo root. I reproduced it with two base dirs: the second open() succeeded while the first store was still open. test_same_account_market_is_locked_even_with_another_database_path (test_ng_store_open_lock.py:69-75) passes only because line 72 forces `other.locks = env.locks`, so it never tests the default layout the handoff tells WS-D to use (open() without lock_dir). The module docstring's 'host-wide lock directory' is not true by default.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Put the account+market lock in a fixed host-wide location that does not depend on data_path (for example ~/.hummingbot/neutral_grid/locks or /var/tmp). Change the test to open two stores with different data paths and the default lock_dir.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this claim. The code shows the gap and I reproduced it.

1. **The spec requires a host-wide lock.** NG-DB-001 (spec line 174) says the account+market lock stops a second engine from starting on the same host. Section 1 excludes only exclusivity across different hosts. Two installs or worktrees on one host are still one host, so they are in scope.

2. **The default lock depends on the checkout.** `default_lock_dir()` (store.py:447-451) returns `data_path()/neutral_grid/locks`. In `hummingbot/__init__.py`, `data_path()` is `realpath(prefix_path()/data)` and `prefix_path` is the repo root. `open()` (store.py:1219) uses that default whenever `lock_dir` is None. The WS-D handoff in trace/ws-b-store.md step 1 tells the engine to call `open()` without `lock_dir`. No other code in the branch passes a host-wide `lock_dir`.

3. **Reproduced.** I ran two processes, each calling `set_data_path` on its own directory (a/ and b/) with the same `EngineIdentity` (domain, account 7, LIT-USDG). Process A opened the store and held it. Process B opened successfully while A was still running, with a different lock file and a different DB. A third open on a/ was correctly refused with `StoreLockedError`. So the lock only works within one data path.

4. **CIDs collide as well.** A fresh DB sets `cid_epoch = 1` (store.py:1404) unless a marker under its own lock_dir or data dir says otherwise. Each checkout has its own markers, so both engines allocate the same `epoch<<40|seq` CIDs on the same account. The `prior_run_markers` callback does not reliably prevent this: it is optional, and it sees nothing when both engines start fresh at about the same time.

5. **The tests hide the gap.** The test `Env` puts locks at `tmp/locks`, outside `tmp/data`, which does not match the default layout. `test_same_account_market_is_locked_even_with_another_database_path` only passes because it sets `other.locks = env.locks` by hand. No test checks the default `lock_dir` with two data paths. The module docstring's claim of a "host-wide lock directory" is false by default.

**Failure scenario:** two Hummingbot checkouts on one host (this user already has several worktrees) both start the neutral grid for the same account and market. Both engines trade the same account, and their CIDs collide. That violates NG-DB-001 and the single-writer/CID guarantees.

**Severity:** high. It needs two installs on one host, but that is exactly what this lock exists to stop, and the result is duplicate exposure plus CID collisions.

confirmed.title: Prior-run 'host marker' is inside the data dir: wiping data/neutral_grid makes a fresh DB, a new baseline and reused CIDs
confirmed.failure_scenario: In the default layout the DB is data/neutral_grid/<key>.sqlite3 and the host marker is data/neutral_grid/locks/<key>.marker.json. The operator deletes data/neutral_grid (or data/) after the DB is lost. The next open(create_if_missing=True) finds no evidence and creates a fresh database with cid_epoch 1. The operator bootstraps a new B, and the first new entry gets the same CID (1<<40|1) as the previous engine's order that may still be live.
confirmed.evidence: _marker_paths (store.py:1335-1336) returns [db_path+'.marker.json', lock_dir/<key>.marker.json], and default_lock_dir and default_db_path share <data_path>/neutral_grid. I reproduced it with the default layout: after rmtree(base/'neutral_grid'), open(create=True) succeeded with epoch 1, bootstrapped=False, and the new entry CID 1099511627777 equalled the old live order's CID. test_wiped_data_directory_still_blocked_by_host_marker (test_ng_store_prior_run.py:65-70) passes only because the Env fixture (ng_store_support.py:69-70) puts locks at tmp/locks, outside tmp/data. That hides the production layout.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Keep the host marker outside data_path (the same host-wide location as the lock) and add a test that uses default_db_path/default_lock_dir with a shared base_dir.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute the claim, and I reproduced it at 39022a497. `_marker_paths` (store.py:1335-1336) is identical in the worktree HEAD. It returns `<db>.marker.json` and `<lock_dir>/<key>.marker.json`. When `lock_dir` is omitted, `open()` uses `default_lock_dir()` (store.py:447-451), which is `<data_path>/neutral_grid/locks`. `default_db_path` (store.py:454-459) is `<data_path>/neutral_grid/<key>.sqlite3`. So in the default layout, both markers sit in the same directory tree as the DB. The handoff in trace/ws-b-store.md says to use the default path under `hummingbot.data_path()`.

Reproduction: I used default_db_path/default_lock_dir with a shared base, bootstrapped, submitted one entry (CID 1099511627777), then ran rmtree(base/'neutral_grid'). After that, `open(create_if_missing=True)` succeeded with no PriorRunEvidenceError, cid_epoch 1 and bootstrapped False. A new bootstrap followed by an entry allocated CID 1099511627777 again. `_initialise` hard-codes cid_epoch=1 when there is no marker or recovery.

The workstream's own AC-54 evidence, test_wiped_data_directory_still_blocked_by_host_marker (test_ng_store_prior_run.py:65-70), passes only because the Env fixture (ng_store_support.py:69-70) puts locks at tmp/locks, outside the wiped tmp/data/neutral_grid. So the claimed "host marker survives a data wipe" protection does not exist in the production layout. The scenario is realistic: /data is git-ignored (.gitignore:48), so a reinstall, a `git clean -xdf` or a volume reset removes both markers.

Why I lowered it from high to medium:
- The spec (NG-DB-004/AC-54) requires fail-closed only when there are signs of a prior run. It does not say where a host marker must live.
- The store has a `prior_run_markers` callback for venue evidence (live orders/trades with our CID epoch), and it has foreign-CID collision checks (`note_foreign_cids` / `is_foreign_cid` in allocate_cid). Both are designed to catch total local loss, but WS-D has to wire them, and nothing in this branch does yet.
- The failure also needs `create_if_missing=True` and a new operator-confirmed bootstrap.

So the store-level defense-in-depth that the workstream claims is defeated in the default layout, and the AC-54 trace evidence is misleading. That is concretely reachable, but venue-side checks are designed to catch it, so it is not high.

confirmed.title: migrate_grid ignores obligations on COMPLETE cycles (late fills) and open history conflicts; the 'obligations' test covers only a live order
confirmed.failure_scenario: The entry is partially filled 4 and proven TERMINAL, the TP of 4 is filled and TERMINAL, and the cycle is closed as COMPLETE. A late fill of 1 on the entry arrives: it is applied, the cycle becomes E=5 and X=4, and LATE_FILL plus CUMULATIVE_EXCEEDS_ORDER conflicts open. grid_mutation_blockers() returns [] and migrate_grid() succeeds. The old grid is RETIRED with an unhedged obligation of 1 that can never get a TP, because record_intent requires an OPEN cycle.
confirmed.evidence: grid_mutation_blockers checks E!=X and dust only for `state = 'OPEN'` cycles (store.py:1951). It ignores COMPLETE cycles with late_evidence and unresolved history_conflicts, although the migrate_grid docstring says it is 'refused while the old grid has open orders, reservations, obligations or dust'. I reproduced it: conflicts ['LATE_FILL','CUMULATIVE_EXCEEDS_ORDER'], E=5 X=4 state COMPLETE, blockers [], migrated to grid-b. test_grid_with_open_orders_or_obligations_cannot_be_migrated (test_ng_store_bootstrap_config.py:137-146) only exercises a LIVE entry order, so its 'obligations' claim is unproven.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Block migration for any cycle (OPEN or COMPLETE) of the old grid with entry_filled != exit_filled, late_evidence==1, open history conflicts or unallocated fills. Add a late-fill test.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute the claim, and I reproduced it at the reviewed commit. The same code is at HEAD 41d347fd6.

**The code.** `grid_mutation_blockers` is at store.py:1937-1957. It looks at leg states, ACTIVE reservations and unfinished outbox rows. It checks E!=X and dust only for cycles matched by `grid_id = ? AND state = 'OPEN'` (line 1951). It never looks at cycles with state COMPLETE, `late_evidence`, unresolved `history_conflicts` or unallocated fills. `migrate_grid` (1959-1994) relies only on these blockers. It does not call `entry_blockers()` and does not check whether the market is frozen.

3. A second probe: `record_intent` with allocations summing to 9 against an amount of 10, with the `ValueError` caught. Result: a PENDING SUBMIT outbox row committed, the leg left in INTENT, and the row listed in `unresolved_outbox()`, which means it can be dispatched.

**Why this is the store's problem and not only the caller's**
- CONTRACTS.md:41 calls `record_intent` and `apply_history_batch` "Atomic ops".
- The store's own test `test_swallowed_statement_error_still_prevents_commit` (test_ng_store_persistence_failure.py:130-140) says that a caller ignoring a failure "must not commit a partial transaction". The store enforces that only for SQLite errors, not for its own guard errors.
- The handoff (trace/ws-b-store.md:106, item 7) tells WS-D to expect `InvalidTransitionError` and `EntryBlockedError` from store guards and show them as blockers. That makes catching them inside the tick's transaction a sanctioned pattern, not a stray engine bug.
- The result breaks AC-39's exact, idempotent split: part of an 8-unit fill stays uncredited to its cycle forever. It also breaks the "nothing half-applied" guarantee of NG-HIST-002 and NG-DB-002, and the store's own consistency checks cannot see the damage.

**Why medium and not higher**
- The failure needs two things: the caller passes a bad allocation or cycle state, and the caller swallows the guard error inside the same transaction.
- The common guards (entry blockers, single physical entry, TP headroom) all run before any write. Only the allocation checks and `allocate_fill`'s per-part caps fire after writes.

confirmed.title: record_order_evidence(final=True) lets a non-history (WS/active-list) row become the terminal proof that releases the reservation
confirmed.requirement: NG-HIST-001/NG-HIST-002 (WS, cancel events and active-list disappearance are not terminal proof; terminal release needs the exact history terminal row), handoff forbidden compromises
confirmed.failure_scenario: The engine passes a WS 'canceled' event, normalised as an ExchangeOrderRow, to record_order_evidence(tx, row, final=True). This sets orders.venue_final=1 without any history_inbox row, dedupe key or payload-conflict check. set_leg_state(TERMINAL) then passes the store's 'exact final venue order row' check and releases the reservation, and the cycle can be closed. A late history fill is then treated as late and the cell may already have re-armed.
confirmed.evidence: record_order_evidence (2425-2444) exposes `final: bool` and calls _update_order_from_row(final=final), which sets `venue_final = MAX(venue_final, ?)` (2873-2880). _check_evidence_for TERMINAL (2410-2415) relies only on order.venue_final and venue_filled. verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute the claim. It holds as written, but it only fires when a caller opts in, so I lowered the severity.

Code evidence:
- `store.py` lines 2425-2444: `record_order_evidence(tx, row, *, final=False)` is public. Its docstring says it is the path for an "active (or other non-deduped) order row". It passes `final` directly into `_update_order_from_row(cid, row, final=final)`.
- Lines 2873-2880: `_update_order_from_row` then runs `venue_final = MAX(venue_final, ?)`. This happens without a `history_inbox` row, a dedupe key or a cursor update.

Probe (scratch pytest built on the repo's own `ng_store_support` fixtures):
- A `canceled` order row with zero fill, sent through `record_order_evidence(tx, row)` with the default `final=False`: the later `set_leg_state(TERMINAL)` is correctly refused.
- The same row with `final=True`: `set_leg_state(TERMINAL)` succeeds with `history_inbox` count 0, and the reservation becomes RELEASED with reason "leg TERMINAL: ws".

So the store's own public API lets a WS or cancel event become terminal proof and release the reservation. That contradicts:
- NG-HIST-001: a local cancel/completed event is not terminal proof.
- NG-HIST-002: terminal release needs the exact terminal order row from the atomic inbox/dedupe path.
- The handoff's forbidden compromise at `docs/tasks/claude-neutral-grid.md` line 38.
- The store's own `set_leg_state` docstring and trace doc step 5 ("the store additionally requires the final row").

Per the spec, no legitimate non-history source can produce a final row: active orders are open by definition. That makes `final=True` a bypass with no valid use.

Why I lowered the severity from medium to low:
- No code in this branch calls it with `final=True`. The tests and trace doc step 5 call `record_order_evidence(tx, row)` without it.
- The failure needs the engine (another workstream) to pass `final=True` explicitly. It is reachable through the public API, but it is a latent opt-in bypass of the store's defence-in-depth rather than a path the documented integration takes.
- A later differing history row would still raise "final order row changed" through `_order_row_problems`, but only after the reservation has already been released.

The fix is to remove the parameter, or ignore it on this path.

confirmed.title: A CUMULATIVE_EXCEEDS_ORDER conflict key is reused, so a further excess fill after the operator resolved the first conflict is silently not re-flagged
confirmed.requirement: AC-40 (trade cumulative > order cumulative stops exposure), NG-HIST-002 (conflict -> pause)
confirmed.failure_scenario: The terminal order row says filled=3 and trades sum to 4, which raises CUMULATIVE_EXCEEDS_ORDER. The operator resolves it. A new trade of 2 for the same CID arrives (leg not final, so no LATE_FILL): leg.filled=6 against venue 3. _check_cumulative builds the same key 'CUMULATIVE_EXCEEDS_ORDER:{latest inactive inbox id}:{cid}', INSERT OR IGNORE does nothing, and the returned record is the already-resolved one. No open conflict exists and entry_blockers is empty while the ledger holds 3 more units than the venue order cumulative.
confirmed.evidence: _conflict 2884-2888 uses conflict_key f"{kind}:{inbox_id}:{cid}" with INSERT OR IGNORE. _check_cumulative 3146-3149 derives inbox_id from the last APPLIED order row, which does not change. Probe H: 'second excess: leg filled 6 venue 3 conflicts [(CUMULATIVE_EXCEEDS_ORDER, False, <resolved_at>)] open [] blockers []'.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Include the offending quantity (leg.filled) or the triggering trade inbox id in the key, or re-open/insert a new conflict when the matching conflict is already resolved.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute the claim. I reproduced it with a scratch probe using the branch's own test fixtures (the probe file lives in the scratchpad; nothing in the repo was changed).

How the code behaves:
- `_conflict` (store.py:2882-2896) builds the key `f"{kind}:{inbox_id}:{cid}"` and writes it with INSERT OR IGNORE. If the row already exists, it re-reads that row, which may already be resolved, and returns it with new=False.
- `_check_cumulative` (store.py:3140-3149) takes inbox_id from the most recent APPLIED INACTIVE_ORDERS row for the CID. A terminal order row cannot be replaced: a changed final row becomes an ORDER_MISMATCH or PAYLOAD_MISMATCH conflict instead. So every later excess for the same CID produces the same key.
- `record_manual_reconciliation` (store.py:3395+) lets the operator resolve conflicts without passing `leg_resolutions`.
- `set_leg_state` to TERMINAL is refused while `venue_filled != leg.filled`, so the leg stays LIVE. A later trade is therefore not late (`late = leg.final or cycle COMPLETE`) and raises no LATE_FILL conflict with a fresh key.
- The OVERFILL check only compares against `leg.amount`, which is 10 in the fixture.

Probe (fixture leg amount 10, state LIVE):
1. Terminal order row with filled=3, then trade t-1 of size 4. Result: CUMULATIVE_EXCEEDS_ORDER with new=True.
2. The operator resolves that conflict with no leg resolution. The leg stays LIVE with filled=4.
3. Trade t-2 of size 2. Result: `[('CUMULATIVE_EXCEEDS_ORDER', False, 1700000001000)]`, meaning the returned record is already resolved. No late fills. Leg filled=6 against venue 3. `open_conflicts()` returns [] and `entry_blockers()` returns [].

Why this breaks the spec: AC-40 says trade cumulative above order cumulative stops exposure. NG-HIST-002 says a conflict means pause. Here the new excess fill is a fact the operator never saw, yet the store leaves no open conflict and no entry blocker, so new ENTRY intents are allowed. The branch contains only store.py, contracts.py and migrations; no engine code checks the returned conflicts in any other way, and `entry_blockers` is the store's persistence gate. The trace file (docs/neutral-grid/trace/ws-b-store.md) marks AC-40 persistence as done, but its test (`test_trade_cumulative_above_terminal_order_cumulative_is_conflict`) only covers the first detection.

Severity: medium. It needs an operator resolution that does not finalize the leg, followed by more inconsistent venue data, but it silently reopens new exposure.

confirmed.title: An ENTRY intent may carry allocations across several cycles, so the store accepts physically glued entries
confirmed.requirement: NG-CELL-002 (one physical entry per cycle; entries must not be glued)
confirmed.failure_scenario: record_intent(entry_leg(3), amount 20, allocations=[(g,3,1,10),(g,4,1,10)]) is accepted. The fills are later split with allocate_fill into cycle 4's entry_filled even though cycle 4 has no own entry leg. The one-physical-entry guard (_check_single_physical_entry) sees only cycle 3, so cycle 4 can also get its own ENTRY and hold two physical entries worth of E.
confirmed.evidence: record_intent 2520-2524 runs _check_single_physical_entry only for the leg's own cycle, then 2540-2541 `if allocations: self._insert_allocations(...)` regardless of role. Probe C: 'ENTRY glued across cells 3 and 4 accepted, amount 20'.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this. The failure scenario is reachable, and I reproduced it.

**The code.** In store.py:2520-2526, `record_intent` runs `_check_single_physical_entry(cycle)` for ENTRY legs, but only against the leg's own cycle. Then at 2540-2541 it runs `if allocations: self._insert_allocations(cid, amount, allocations)` whatever the role is. `_insert_allocations` (2609-2621) checks only three things: each part is positive, each target cycle is OPEN, and the parts sum to the amount. It does not reject role == ENTRY. It also does not check that a target cycle has the same entry side or price as the leg's cell.

**How the fill gets credited.** In `_apply_trade_row` (around line 3099), a CID that has allocations is not credited to its own cycle. `allocate_fill` (3209-3243) then calls `_credit_cycle(target, fill.role=ENTRY, amount)` for each target cycle. `_check_single_physical_entry` (2546-2556) looks only at legs whose grid/cell/generation match the cycle. So a cycle whose entry quantity came only through an allocation still counts as having no entry leg.

**Probe.** I ran a script using the repo's test helpers (`Env`, `bootstrap`, `FakeTransport`) against the repo's Python env, with no network. The result:
- An ENTRY on cell 3 (BUY @ 5.0545, amount 20) with allocations `[(g,3,1,10), (g,4,1,10)]` was accepted.
- After the fill of 20 and `allocate_fill`, cycle 4 had E=10 and cycle 3 had E=10. Cell 4's own entry price is 5.0727, so cycle 4 was credited with entry quantity filled at another cell's price.
- A separate `prepare_submit` of an ENTRY for `entry_leg(4)` of 10 was then also accepted. Cycle 4 now has two physical entries' worth of exposure.
- `verify_ledger()` returned `[]`, so the store did not detect the inconsistency.

**Spec.** NG-CELL-002 (spec line 78) says: "В MVP один cycle имеет один physical entry order; нельзя склеивать entries". Spec line 40 and AC-39/AC-33 allow aggregation only for same-side, same-target remainders, meaning TP or dust, and never entries.

**Scope.** This is in the workstream's scope. Its own trace, docs/neutral-grid/trace/ws-b-store.md lines 36 and 53, lists "one physical entry per cycle" and fixed side/price per role as store-level guards under NG-CELL-001/002/003 (persistence). The AC-39 persistence test covers only a TP with allocations. No store check rejects an ENTRY with allocations, so a WS-A caller bug is not caught by the promised safety net.

**Severity.** Medium is appropriate. Reaching this needs a caller to pass allocations on an ENTRY, but the store's advertised guard against doubled entry exposure can be bypassed, and the ledger check does not flag it.

**Fix.** Reject allocations when role == ENTRY. For TP allocations, also require every target cycle to share the leg's side and target price.

refuted.title: Trade dedupe key falls back to empty own_exchange_order_id, so the same trade is applied twice
refuted.why:
The store code does what the claim says, but the failure scenario can't happen with real venue data, and the part that would let it happen sits outside WS-B.

1. **The mechanism is real.** I ran a probe against the store (same dedupe/apply code at 39022a497 and HEAD). With submit UNKNOWN, amount 6, and trade t-77 of size 3 sent first with own_exchange_order_id=None and later with '555': two new fills, no conflicts, leg.filled=6, cycle entry_filled=6, entry_blockers=[]. The only guards are OVERFILL (leg.filled+size>amount) and _check_cumulative once a terminal order row arrives.

2. **The store uses the spec's own key.** NG-HIST-002 defines the canonical trade key as (domain, account, market, trade_id_str, own_side, own_exchange_order_id). store.py:366 only wraps `ExchangeTradeRow.dedupe_key()`. That method, including the `own_exchange_order_id or ""` part, lives in contracts.py. contracts.py was frozen in base commit a18cb37d4 ("workstream contracts and shared types"), not in WS-B. Under the spec's literal key, rows with different own_exchange_order_id are different keys. The "fallback only on exact typed SDK IDs" clause means using `ask_id` when `ask_id_str` is missing, and the connector already does that via `_agreeing_id(raw, ("ask_id_str","ask_id"))`.

3. **The scenario can't be reached with real data.** own_exchange_order_id is None only if the venue sends neither `{side}_id_str` nor `{side}_id` for a trade. In the pinned lighter SDK (the installed `lighter/models/trade.py`), the Trade model declares `ask_id: StrictInt` and `bid_id: StrictInt` as required. Only the `_id_str` variants are Optional. So every schema-conforming /api/v1/trades row carries the own order id, and `trade_rows_from_raw` on codex/ng-connector always yields a non-None, stable own_exchange_order_id. This is the only producer of rows passed to apply_history_batch; the engine's `_trade_from_fill` / `_load_committed` rebuild rows from store data and don't re-apply them. The claimed sequence (same trade first without an order id, then with one) needs the venue to break its own schema. Under NG-HIST-002 ("schema conflict ... делают history incomplete"), such a row should be rejected at the connector/scanner layer. That layer's `required=False` for the order id is a connector-workstream (WS-C) issue, not a WS-B store defect.

4. **What's left is hardening.** The store could refuse owned trade rows with no exchange order id. That is defense in depth against a non-conforming venue, not a violation of an NG-*/AC-* clause that a real sequence triggers. If it were kept at all, it would be low severity and would belong to the connector/contract owners.

refuted.title: Restoring an older DB backup silently rewinds the CID counter and re-issues CIDs already sent to the venue
refuted.why:
The code facts in the claim are correct. At 39022a497, `_open_existing` (store.py ~1479-1497) compares only the markers' db_uuid, and the markers have no CID high-water. So a restored T0 backup opens cleanly with `cid_state.next_seq` back at its T0 value. That alone does not break NG-HIST-004 / AC-43, and no spec clause asks the store to detect a stale backup.

1. **The spec does not ask for this.** NG-DB-004 only says the engine stays fail-closed until a backup is restored or an explicit manual reconciliation is done. Nothing requires a CID high-water kept outside the DB or stale-backup detection. The suggested fix is a new design feature.

2. **NG-DB-003 makes restart reconciliation mandatory.** Before any new entries, a restart must read active orders and paginated inactive orders and trades with overlap. The restored cursors sit at T0, so that scan covers everything after T0, including order X.

3. **The store already turns that evidence into a fail-closed collision:**
   - An active X row goes through `record_order_evidence`; since X is not in the restored `cid_map`, it calls `_note_foreign(client, "active_orders")` (store.py ~2433-2439).
   - Inactive X rows and X fills go through `_apply_order_row` / `_apply_trade` and then `_classify_unowned`, which also calls `_note_foreign` (store.py ~3010-3013, 3097-3102). Post-cut X fills also become UNMATCHED inbox rows, and `entry_blockers` blocks new entries on those.
   - `allocate_cid` then raises `CidCollisionError` when the candidate is in `foreign_cids` or `is_foreign_cid` rejects it (store.py ~2276-2280).
   - This exact path is tested: `test_ng_store_cid.py::test_collision_from_history_evidence_and_caller_check` records a history trade carrying the next candidate CID, and `allocate_cid` fails closed. The trace doc's handoff also names `prior_run_markers` / `is_foreign_cid` as the caller-side checks.

4. **The probe skipped the mandatory step.** It restored the backup and allocated for cell 7 without ingesting any venue evidence. That is an engine skipping NG-DB-003, not a store defect.

5. **The leftover cases do not produce the claimed harm:**
   - If X never reached the venue, there is no active row or fill to misattribute.
   - If X's evidence is older than the venue's history retention, that is the AC-53 retention-gap / manual-reconcile path, which the handoff assigns to WS-C/WS-D.

The claimed misattribution of X's rows or fills to cell 7 cannot happen once the spec-mandated restart reconciliation runs.

refuted.title: Q is not immutable per cycle: open_cycle accepts planned_amount override and ENTRY intents accept any amount
refuted.why:
The code does what the claim says: open_cycle (store.py:2146-2149) accepts an optional planned_amount, and record_intent for an ENTRY (2517-2524) checks side, price, entry blockers and the single physical entry, but not the amount. That is not a defect under the clauses the claim cites.

1) NG-ARCH-003 and AC-52 are about config mutation: "Grid dimensions/Q нельзя менять у работающего grid" and "Running grid dimensions/Q отклоняются". The store already enforces this. The grids row (which holds order_amount_base) is immutable by trigger. A changed config fingerprint is rejected at open and at revision (test_changed_dimensions_are_rejected_at_open_and_revision). Migration is audited and keeps old cycles. In the claim's scenario the grid's Q stays 10 and no config is mutated. What it describes is a per-order sizing bug in the caller, not a Q change on a running grid.

2) AC-07 and the "new cycle uses the full order_amount_base" rule in NG-CELL-001/003 belong to the cell ledger and engine workstream, not WS-B. CONTRACTS.md gives WS-B ACs 15, 16, 18, 19, 22, 43, 52, 53, 54 and 55, not AC-07. It defines record_intent as record_intent(tx, leg_identity, submit_request, reservation), with no amount-vs-Q validation. Amount decisions sit with cells.CellLedger and the engine. The store's price/side guard is extra protection the spec does not demand. A missing extra guard does not break any WS-B clause.

3) The failure scenario cannot be reached in this branch. Nothing passes planned_amount: grep finds it only inside store.py. The only test call uses the default and asserts planned_amount == 10. No engine code here sends an ENTRY that differs from Q. The scenario needs a hypothetical future bug ("the engine, or a config-reload bug"), so this is a "consider adding a guard" suggestion, not a concrete defect.

If it were kept at all, it would be low-severity hardening, meaning drop the unused planned_amount parameter, not a medium violation of NG-ARCH-003 or AC-52.

refuted.title: After a restart, a DISPATCHED submit can be recorded as NOT_SENT or zero-fill reject: an unknown outcome is treated as proven absence
refuted.why:
The code does behave as the reviewer says. At store.py:2747 (same line at 39022a497), only PENDING rows reject results other than NOT_SENT, so NOT_SENT on a DISPATCHED row is accepted. It is still not a store defect under the spec.

1. NOT_SENT on a DISPATCHED row is a legitimate in-process path, so the store cannot reject it outright. The port contract has submit() do pre-send validation after mark_dispatching has committed. The codex/ng-engine lighter_port.submit returns TransportResult(NOT_SENT, "pre_send_validation: ...") for a non-SubmitRequest, reduce_only or an unsupported type/side. These return before connector.submit_with_client_id is called. Any exception from the connector is mapped to UNKNOWN. The store records what transport reported; it cannot check transport results in-process either.

2. The failure scenario needs a caller that makes up a transport result for a call it never made. The real engine (codex/ng-engine engine.py) does not do this:
   - `_close_open_outbox` records NOT_SENT only for `row.status == "PENDING"` and UNKNOWN for every other status ("NOT_SENT only for a never-dispatched PENDING row").
   - `_dispatch_intent` records NOT_SENT only before mark_dispatching, when `_pre_send_blocker` fires; otherwise it records the port's own result.
   - `_withdraw` acts only when `leg.state == INTENT`, meaning the row was never dispatched.
   - The engine never uses resend_same_cid.

   So the restart path from the claim, where the engine calls record_transport_result(NOT_SENT) on an inherited DISPATCHED row, cannot be reached with the actual components.

3. No spec or contract clause asks for this guard. NG-DB-005 puts the "proof that transport was not called" on whoever knows whether transport was called. CONTRACTS.md defines only `record_transport_result(tx, cid, result)`. AC-16 requires that a restart sees the outbox ID, issues no new ID, and does not present ambiguity as absence.

The store's recovery surfaces already meet AC-16, as test_ac16_crash_after_dispatch_mark_is_ambiguous_not_absent shows. After restart:
   - the DISPATCHED row reports transport_possibly_invoked=True;
   - the leg stays SUBMIT_UNKNOWN;
   - the reservation is kept;
   - allocate_cid returns the same CID;
   - set_leg_state(TERMINAL) without evidence is refused.

The trace doc's open risks say plainly that the store enforces the result side of the protocol, not the call itself. It also tells the engine that DISPATCHED/UNKNOWN rows stay SUBMIT_UNKNOWN until history/active evidence or an audited manual reconciliation.

Tagging each row with the owner that dispatched it would be extra defense, not a missing requirement, and no concrete reachable failure follows from its absence.

refuted.title: mark_dispatching on a DISPATCHED row left by a dead process returns success, so the same-CID resend path skips the resend_same_cid gate
refuted.why:
The code does what the claim says. At 39022a497, store.py:2667-2668 returns a DISPATCHED row unchanged, the resend_same_cid gate covers only DONE rows, and a DISPATCHED row survives restart (test_ac16_crash_after_dispatch_mark_is_ambiguous_not_absent). The failure scenario still does not hold, for four reasons.

1. It misstates the documented protocol. The claim says the engine "follows the reference protocol for unresolved_outbox rows (mark_dispatching, then port.submit)". The handoff says otherwise (docs/neutral-grid/trace/ws-b-store.md:91-93). After restart only PENDING rows may be dispatched. DISPATCHED/UNKNOWN rows "stay SUBMIT_UNKNOWN with reservation until history/active evidence or audited manual reconciliation". Same-CID resend is allowed only through resend_same_cid=True with documented venue idempotence. The reference helper submit_via_protocol is for a freshly committed intent, not for recovering DISPATCHED rows. An engine that follows the documented protocol never calls mark_dispatching on a DISPATCHED row and never resends it.

2. The store does not send anything and says it does not police transport calls. The same-CID resend happens only when engine code (WS-D) calls port.submit. The WS-B open risks (trace:136-137) state that "the store enforces the result side of that protocol, not the call itself". For a DISPATCHED row, mark_dispatching is a no-op: no state change, no new CID, the reservation is kept, the leg stays SUBMIT_UNKNOWN. Raising there would not stop an engine that ignores the protocol, because it could call port.submit on entry.request anyway. The "blind retry" comes entirely from engine code that breaks its contract, which is outside WS-B.

3. The spec clause is met by the store's actual duties. NG-HIST-004 and NG-DB-002 forbid a new ID after timeout or crash (enforced: allocate_cid returns the same CID after restart, and prepare_submit/record_intent reuse the mapped CID). They also require that ambiguity is not reported as absence (enforced: leg stays SUBMIT_UNKNOWN, reservation kept, TERMINAL/zero-fill guesses refused). "Same ID only with documented venue idempotence" is a policy on when the engine sends. No clause requires the store's mark_dispatching to refuse a no-op call on an already-DISPATCHED row. AC-16 requires only that restart sees the outbox ID, issues no new ID, and does not report ambiguity as absence, and the tests cover exactly that.

4. No engine exists on this branch. So no current code path calls mark_dispatching on a DISPATCHED row and then transports; the scenario needs future WS-D code that contradicts the handoff.

What remains is a hardening point. The DISPATCHED/DONE-UNKNOWN gate is asymmetric, and a legitimate audited resend of a DISPATCHED row through resend_same_cid=True does not increment attempts. That is at most low severity, not the spec violation claimed.

refuted.title: The immutable-dimension guard trusts only the caller's fingerprint: dimension changes with the old fingerprint are recorded, and open() without a fingerprint skips the check
refuted.why:
The reproduction works as described, but it does not show a violation of AC-52, NG-ARCH-003 or NG-DB-003 in this workstream.

1. The fingerprint is the dimension identity the contract defines. The frozen shared contract says so in contracts.py:134: `GridConfig.fingerprint()` is the "Stable identity of grid dimensions (bounds, N, Q, pair, account). Implemented by core." WS-A computes it from the config's own dimensions. If a dimension changes, the fingerprint changes. Scenario 1 needs a caller that passes a fingerprint that does not match the config it passes alongside it. That is a caller breaking the contract, not a store defect. `config` is typed `Any` and is stored as canonical JSON, so the store has no schema to check dimensions against. The store also cannot compute the fingerprint itself, because core owns the algorithm. That is why the test uses opaque fingerprint strings.

2. The running grid's dimensions cannot change through this path. Dimensions and Q live in the `grids` row. That row is protected by SQLite triggers (`grids_dimensions_immutable` and `grids_no_delete` in m0001_initial.py:135-142). The only way to replace them is `migrate_grid()`, which is audited and allowed only on a quiescent grid. `bootstrap()` cannot run twice. The reviewer's own check shows `grid().cell_count` staying at 55, so the immutability AC-52 requires holds.

3. The recorded `config_json` is audit-only and never read. store.py has no SELECT against config_revisions. It only inserts rows, at lines 1875, 1929 and 1980. Nothing, including restart, load_state or snapshots, takes grid dimensions from that JSON. So "the latest recorded config claims other dimensions" does not change any store behaviour.

4. The `config_fingerprint=None` default on `open()` is an integration concern for WS-D. The WS-B handoff in trace/ws-b-store.md:81 tells the engine to call `open(..., config_fingerprint=config.fingerprint())`. When the fingerprint is supplied, the store rejects a mismatch before any write (store.py:1488-1492), and a test covers that. NG-DB-003 step 1 is part of the engine's restart procedure. For it to fail, WS-D would have to leave out a documented argument, and no code in this workstream does that. Even with None, the store's grid row stays immutable, and every later dimension change is still blocked by `record_config_revision` and `migrate_grid`.

Neither scenario can be reached through a defect in the store, migrations or tests. Both need an out-of-scope caller to break the documented contract.

refuted.title: The AC-19 'mid_history_batch' crash case is vacuous, and the crashed batch's ledger transition is a no-op
refuted.why:
The facts in the claim are right, but they describe how strong one test parameter is. They do not show a product defect or an unmet AC-19 or NG-HIST-002 clause.

What checks out at 39022a497:
- In store.py, apply_history_batch sets `midpoint = len(rows)//2`, which is 1. It hits "mid_history_batch" before row index 1 (t-2) is applied.
- Row 0 is the duplicate t-1. The duplicate path only reads dedupe_keys and history_inbox and returns without writing. So when the mid-batch crash fires, nothing new has been written.
- The leg is already LIVE from the FakeTransport ACCEPTED result, so `set_leg_state(LIVE)` returns early at `if leg.state == to_state`.
- In the mid_history_batch case the ledger_transitions are never reached at all.

Why this is not a reportable defect:
1. **AC-19 is covered.** The spec's AC-19 is "Crash before cursor commit": inbox, ledger and cursor roll back together, and replay neither loses nor doubles a fill. The before_cursor_commit parameter of the same test does exactly this. t-2 and t-3 are inserted into the inbox and dedupe keys, fills are attributed and leg.filled rises to 9, the transitions run, and then the crash fires. The reopened store shows filled == 4, only fill t-1, and cursor c-1. Replay is then idempotent. The before_commit parameter repeats this at the last moment before COMMIT. The claim itself concedes AC-19 is covered.
2. **The failure scenario does not hold for the test as a whole.** A store that committed each history row separately would pass the mid_history_batch parameter. It would fail the before_cursor_commit and before_commit parameters of the same test, because t-2 and t-3 would persist. So the regression the claim describes would still be caught.
3. **No product failure is reachable.** The rows, `_check_cumulative`, the transitions and the cursor updates all run inside one `self._scope(tx)`. There is a single SQLite transaction, and no path applies engine transitions outside it. The only gap is that a no-op LegStateChange never exercises rollback of a state-changing engine transition. That is a hypothetical future regression, not current wrong behaviour.
4. **The handoff's crash-injection requirement is met.** It asks for crash injection across all persistence windows. The rows-written window is injected and asserted at before_cursor_commit and before_commit. A crash between rows leaves a subset of that state, so the stronger cases dominate it.

The suggested fix is a "consider strengthening the test" item, which the review scope excludes. The one real inaccuracy is that trace/ws-b-store.md line 60 lists "mid batch" coverage. That is a minor documentation overstatement, not a defect.

I ran the three ac19 parameters read-only and they pass.

refuted.title: prepare_submit, the handoff's reference submit path, cannot pass is_foreign_cid, so the caller collision check claimed for AC-43 is unreachable there
refuted.why: Refuted. The claim is that the caller collision check can't be reached from prepare_submit. It can, and the failure scenario doesn't happen on the documented path. (1) prepare_submit (store.py:2598-2606) is only a convenience wrapper for allocate_cid + record_intent. allocate_cid is idempotent per leg identity: it returns the existing CID when cid_for(leg) is set (store.py:2257-2259). So an engine that wants the callback calls `store.allocate_cid(tx, leg, is_foreign_cid=cb)` and then `prepare_submit(tx, leg, ...)` in the same transaction. I checked this with a scratch script against the worktree. With a callback that rejects the next candidate, allocate_cid raised CidCollisionError before prepare_submit ran. With a callback that accepts it, prepare_submit returned the same CID that had been checked. CONTRACTS.md:41 names allocate_cid(tx, leg_identity) and record_intent as the atomic ops; prepare_submit is not in the contract. (2) The scenario says the engine sees the manual order in its active-order scan but the store is never told. That contradicts the handoff. Handoff step 5 (trace/ws-b-store.md) sends active orders through `record_order_evidence(tx, row)`. For an unowned row, that function stores the client id with `_note_foreign(client, "active_orders")` (store.py:2429-2438). In the same scratch run, record_order_evidence was called for an unknown open order carrying the next candidate CID and returned None. The next plain `prepare_submit` then raised CidCollisionError for that CID. History rows are noted the same way through `_classify_unowned` (store.py:3036-3038). (3) NG-HIST-004 and AC-43 require that a collision fails closed and that there is no silent truncate/hash or retry with a new ID. They do not require a callback parameter on any particular wrapper. The store meets this through the durable foreign_cids table, which is filled automatically from active-order and history evidence, plus the optional callback on allocate_cid. The scenario can only happen if WS-D scans active orders and skips the documented record_order_evidence step. That would be an engine wiring bug outside this workstream, not a store defect.

refuted.title: The store persists and dispatches reduce_only=True TP intents
refuted.why:
The claim is correct that store.py:2484-2485 in record_intent only checks that `reduce_only` is a bool and would store a request with reduce_only=True. But the failure it describes, a reduce-only TP reaching the venue, cannot happen, and no spec clause makes this a store duty.

1) The store never sends anything. mark_dispatching (store.py:2656-2690) only marks the outbox row DISPATCHED and the leg SUBMIT_UNKNOWN. Sending is done by the engine and the connector port.

2) Every sending path has its own guard against reduce_only:
   - WS-D engine.py (codex/ng-engine) `_submit` always builds the request with `reduce_only=False` (~line 1566).
   - WS-D `_pre_send_blocker` (engine.py:1524) returns "REDUCE_ONLY_FORBIDDEN" if `req.reduce_only` is set.
   - WS-C lighter_port.py:396 (codex/ng-connector) returns NOT_SENT for any request with reduce_only not False ("neutral grid never sends reduce_only").
   - The connector's `submit_with_client_id` (lighter_perpetual_derivative.py:1663) passes `reduce_only=False` explicitly, as CONTRACTS.md requires.
   - WS-A cells.py also builds the request with `reduce_only=False` (line ~775 on codex/ng-core).
   A reduce-only TP would need several separate bugs in other workstreams at once. Even then the port and connector would refuse it or send it with reduce_only=False.

3) What the spec requires: NG-ORD-002 says entry and TP orders are ordinary orders with reduce_only=false and that PositionAction.CLOSE must not be used blindly. The handoff says not to make the virtual TP reduce-only. Both are about how orders are built and sent, which WS-A, WS-C and WS-D own. Neither says the persistence layer must reject the flag.
   - The store's contract section in CONTRACTS.md lists record_intent's atomicity duties and says nothing about validating reduce_only.
   - The trace file's "Store-level guards" row calls the store an optional safety net and lists specific checks (fixed side/price, TP headroom, and others). reduce_only is not among them, so this is not a false traceability claim either.

Result: storing the value unvalidated is at most extra hardening, not a defect with a reachable failure in this workstream.

refuted.title: The ENTRY amount is not bound to the cycle's planned amount or Q, so a rounded-up or non-Q entry is durably accepted
refuted.why:
The code description is accurate, but the requirement it cites does not belong to this workstream. record_intent's ENTRY branch (store.py ~2520-2524) checks only blockers and the single-physical-entry rule, and open_cycle (2146-2149) accepts any positive planned_amount, defaulting to grid.order_amount_base. That does not violate any clause the WS-B store owns.

(1) AC-23 and NG-GRID-003 (quantity never rounded up, size-step multiples) are assigned to WS-A core in CONTRACTS.md. The WS-A row lists "23–28", and cells.tp_obligation_to_dispatch is specified as "never rounded up". The WS-B AC list is 15, 16, 18, 19, 22(DB), 43(durable), 52, 53(persist), 54, 55, with no AC-23. The review brief's scope list also has neither NG-GRID-003 nor NG-CELL-001's cycle-sizing rule.

(2) NG-CELL-001 line 72 ("a new cycle of the full order_amount_base") describes the engine's behaviour. In the store, the only claimed persistence part of NG-CELL-001/002/003 is the whole-cell lock, one physical entry, X + reserved TP <= E, and same-side rearm (trace line 53: "store guards done; FSM is WS-A/WS-D"). The store enforces all of these. The trace (line 36) describes the store guards as a "persistence-derivable safety net under WS-A/WS-D logic". It never claims to bind the entry amount to Q.

(3) The store's default path already persists planned_amount = grid.order_amount_base. NG-GRID-003 requires order_amount_base to be an exact size-step multiple and has the config rejected otherwise. A rounded-up entry is therefore possible only if WS-A/WS-D contains the bug the claim invents ("engine quantizes Q=10 up to 10.1 because of a size-step bug"). The store still records exactly the amount it was given. A missing extra guard against another component's hypothetical bug is a defense-in-depth suggestion, not a defect in this workstream. No spec clause requires the persistence layer to reject amount != Q.
